summary: Describes an optional extension to the Internet Printing Protocol 1.1 that lets a client subscribe to printing events, modeled as Subscription Objects that say what to do when a given event occurs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3995 lets a print client ask a printer to tell it when something happens, for example when a job finishes or the printer runs out of paper. The client names the events it cares about and where the messages should go, and the printer keeps a record of that request. When an event happens the printer sends a message, either straight away or waiting for the client to ask for it.

questions: how to subscribe to printer events
what is the ippget delivery method
how long does an ipp subscription last
subtitle: How a print client asks a printer to report job and printer events, and how long that request lasts.

tldr.problem: The Internet Printing Protocol lets a client submit a print job and ask about it later, but the protocol has no way for the printer to tell the client that something has changed while the client waits, such as a paper jam or the job finishing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds Subscription Objects. A client sends a subscription creation operation naming the events it wants, where the notification should go and how to deliver it. The printer creates an object for each subscription, and when a matching event occurs it sends an Event Notification to the recipient, either pushing it or holding it for the recipient to pull.
tldr.outcome: Six new IPP operations are defined, of which five must be supported, and the ippget pull delivery method is required so that every conforming implementation can be reached the same way. A per-printer subscription lasts for a lease that the client has to renew, and the memo caps that lease at about two years, while a per-job subscription simply ends with its job.

facts.label: Lease duration range
facts.value: 0 to 67108863 seconds, where 0 means the lease never expires

facts.label: notify-time-interval
facts.value: Any nonnegative integer, the minimum seconds between job-progress notifications

facts.label: notify-user-data
facts.value: At most 63 octets of opaque data

today: RFC 3995 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level. It updates RFC 2911 and RFC 2910, the Internet Printing Protocol version 1.1 model and encoding, by adding an optional extension for event notifications, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
RFC 3995 is an optional extension to the Internet Printing Protocol version 1.1, the model and semantics of RFC 2911 and the encoding and transport of RFC 2910. Together with the IPP job progress attributes of RFC 3381 and the ippget delivery method of RFC 3996, it is intended to meet the most important notification requirements described in RFC 3997.

The specification requires that clients and printers support the ippget pull delivery method, and conforming implementations may support additional push or pull delivery methods. The memo defines no delivery method of its own, but it does define the rules for the conformance of delivery method documents and their registration with IANA.

The document defines operations a client can perform to create Subscription Objects in a printer and to carry out other operations on them. A Subscription Object represents a Subscription abstraction: it specifies that when one of the specified events occurs, the printer delivers an asynchronous Event Notification to the specified Notification Recipient via the specified delivery method, which is a protocol.

When a client, called a subscribing client, performs an operation that creates a Subscription Object, the operation contains one or more Subscription Template Attributes Groups. Each such group holds the information the printer uses to initialize a newly created Subscription Object, and the printer creates one Subscription Object for each group. The group works like the Job Template Attributes group of RFC 2911. A group typically holds the names of the subscribed events of interest, the address of one notification recipient for a push delivery method or the method for a pull delivery method, the delivery method itself, some opaque data that the printer delivers to the recipient, the charset to use in text fields, the natural language to use in those fields, and the requested lease time in seconds for the Subscription Object.

There are three kinds of subscription creation operation. A Job Creation operation, that is Print-Job, Print-URI or Create-Job, can carry zero or more subscription template groups in the request, and the printer creates one Subscription Object for each and associates it with the newly created job. The Create-Job-Subscriptions operation creates Subscription Objects associated with the job that is the target of the operation. The Create-Printer-Subscriptions operation creates Subscription Objects associated with the printer that is the target of the operation.

A Subscription Object associated with a job is called a Per-Job Subscription Object, and one associated with the printer is called a Per-Printer Subscription Object. The response contains one Subscription Attributes Group for each template group in the request, in the same order, and a successfully created Subscription Object's group contains the notify-subscription-id attribute, which uniquely identifies it and is analogous to a job-id for a Job object.

Four more operations are defined: Restart-Job, where the printer reuses the same job and its Subscription Objects; Validate-Job, where a client can ask whether Subscription Objects could be created without creating them; Get-Subscription-Attributes, which returns the attributes of a target Subscription Object; Get-Subscriptions, which returns the attributes of all Subscription Objects associated with the printer or a specified job; Renew-Subscription, which renews the lease on a Per-Printer Subscription Object before it expires; and Cancel-Subscription, which cancels the lease or deletes the object.

When an event occurs, the printer finds all the Subscription Objects listening for it. For each one it generates an Event Notification, and then either delivers it straight away, if the delivery method is a push method as shown by the presence of the notify-recipient-uri attribute, or saves it for a period called the Event Life, if the delivery method is a pull method as shown by the presence of the notify-pull-method attribute, in which case the recipient is expected to fetch the notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds a way for a printer to report changes to a client that asked about them. The client lists the events it wants in a subscription request, the printer keeps that request as a Subscription Object, and the printer sends a message when one of those events happens.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The memo defines the terms it uses, on top of the terms of RFC 2911 such as client, Printer, attribute, attribute value, keyword, operation, request, response, administrator, operator and support.

An Event is some occurrence, expected or unexpected, within the printing system of a change of state, condition or configuration of a job or printer object. An event occurs only at one instant in time and does not span the time the physical event takes place, so jam-occurred and jam-cleared are two distinct, instantaneous events even though the jam may last a while.

An Event Notification is the information about an event that the printer delivers when the event occurs. The attributes group used to deliver it is the Event Notification Attributes Group, used in a request for push delivery methods and in a response for pull ones. A Machine Consumable Event Notification is bytes for program consumption, formatted according to the delivery method document. A Human Consumable Event Notification is localized text for human consumption only, with no standardized format, so programs should not try to parse it.

A Delivery Method is the mechanism, that is the protocol, by which the printer delivers an Event Notification. Each one is defined in a Delivery Method Document separate from the memo. A Push Delivery Method is one where the printer delivers the notification shortly after the event occurs. A Pull Delivery Method is one where the printer saves the notifications for an Event Life time and expects the recipient to request them, delivering them in a response to such a request. The Event Life is the length of time in seconds after an event during which the printer will retain that event for delivery; once it expires the printer no longer delivers a notification for that event in such a response.

A Notification Recipient is the entity to which the printer delivers an Event Notification. For push methods the printer sends the notification to it; for pull methods the recipient acts in the role of an IPP client and requests the notifications, so the two terms are used interchangeably there. A Compound Event Notification is two or more Event Notifications that the printer delivers together as a single request or response, and the delivery method document says whether the method supports them.

Events are split into Job Events, caused by some change in a particular job such as job-completed, and Printer Events, caused by some change in the printer that is not specific to a job, such as printer-state-changed.
sections.plainLanguage: An event is a single instant, not a period, so a jam starting and a jam clearing are two different events. A delivery method is the way the message travels: either the printer pushes it out, or it keeps it and the recipient fetches it.

sections.title: The Object Model
sections.content:
The object model adds a Subscription Object, which together with the Job and Printer objects give the complete notification semantics. The object relationships are given by example. A Printer object contains, or is associated with, zero or more Per-Printer Subscription Objects, and each Per-Printer Subscription Object is contained in, or associated with, exactly one Printer object. A Job object is associated with zero or more Per-Job Subscription Objects, and each Per-Job Subscription Object is associated with exactly one Job object. Whether the objects are really contained or merely associated is implementation dependent and transparent to the client.

Per-Job and Per-Printer Subscription Objects are quite similar. Either type can subscribe to Job Events, Printer Events, or both. Both can be queried with the Get-Subscriptions and Get-Subscription-Attributes operations and cancelled with the Cancel-Subscription operation, and both have the same Subscription Object attributes. The differences are these. A client usually creates one or more Per-Job Subscription Objects as part of the Job Creation operations rather than using the optional Create-Job-Subscriptions operation, especially since printer implementations need not support that operation. For Per-Job Subscription Objects the Subscription Object is only valid while the job is not complete, while for Per-Printer Subscription Objects it is valid until the time the printer returned in the notify-lease-expiration-time operation attribute. And Job Events in a Per-Job Subscription Object apply only to one job, the job created by the Job Creation operation or referenced by the Create-Job-Subscriptions operation, while Job Events in a Per-Printer Subscription Object apply to all the jobs in the printer.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of subscription. One hangs off a single print job and dies with it. The other hangs off the whole printer and lives for a fixed time that the client must keep topping up.

sections.title: The Subscription Template Attributes
sections.content:
The Subscription Template Attributes are the values a client supplies when it asks for a subscription, and the printer uses them to fill in the Subscription Object it creates. The memo lists them in Table 1.

The notify-recipient-uri attribute holds the address of one notification recipient for a push delivery method, and its presence is what tells the printer that the method is a push method. The notify-pull-method attribute holds the method for a pull delivery method, and its presence tells the printer that the method is a pull method.

The notify-events attribute is a set of keywords naming the events the client wants to hear about. The registered values are none, then the Printer Events printer-state-changed, printer-restarted, printer-shutdown, printer-stopped, printer-config-changed, printer-media-changed, printer-finishings-changed and printer-queue-order-changed, and then the Job Events job-state-changed, job-created, job-completed, job-stopped, job-config-changed and job-progress.

The notify-attributes attribute is a set of keywords naming the attributes the client wants returned in the event notification, such as job attributes or printer attributes. The notify-user-data attribute carries opaque data, at most 63 octets, that the printer delivers to the notification recipient in the event notification, for example a forwarding address the recipient might use.

The notify-charset attribute gives the charset to use in text fields within an event notification, and notify-natural-language gives the natural language to use in those fields. The notify-lease-duration attribute gives the duration of the lease in seconds; the duration is infinite if the value is 0, that is, the lease never expires, and the attribute is not present on a Per-Job Subscription Object because that object lasts exactly as long as its job. A printer must support this attribute. The client must not supply it when creating a Per-Job Subscription Object, and if it does the printer must treat it as an unsupported attribute. The maximum value of 67,108,863 is 2 to the power of 26 minus 1, which is about 2 years in seconds, and it is set well below the maximum so that there is virtually no chance of an overflow when the printer adds it to its printer-up-time value.

The notify-time-interval attribute lets a subscribing client say how often it wants to be told about job-progress events, which occur each time the printer completes a sheet. The value is any nonnegative integer giving the minimum number of seconds between job-progress notifications. A printer must support this attribute if and only if it supports the job-progress event.
sections.plainLanguage: Each subscription request carries a list of the events the client wants, where the messages should go, and how they should be delivered. It also carries a lease, which is how long the subscription lasts, and an optional setting for how often to be told about print progress.

sections.title: The Subscription Description Attributes
sections.content:
The Subscription Description Attributes are the values the printer reports back about a Subscription Object it has created, and they are what a client reads with Get-Subscription-Attributes and Get-Subscriptions.

The notify-subscription-id attribute is a unique identifier for the Subscription Object, analogous to a job-id for a Job object, and it is what the Renew-Subscription and Cancel-Subscription operations use to name their target. The notify-sequence-number attribute counts the notifications delivered for that Subscription Object, and the notify-lease-expiration-time attribute gives the time in seconds when the lease expires. The notify-printer-up-time attribute gives the printer's up time, notify-printer-uri gives the printer's URI, notify-job-id gives the job a Per-Job Subscription Object belongs to, and notify-subscriber-user-name gives the name of the user who made the subscription.

Two new Printer Description Attributes are added as well: printer-state-change-time, giving the time in seconds since the printer's up time when its state last changed, and printer-state-change-date-time, giving the same as a date and time.

Two attributes appear only inside an event notification. The notify-subscribed-event attribute names the event that the notification is about, and the notify-text attribute holds the human consumable text of the notification.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the values the printer reports back about a subscription: its identifier, how many notifications have been sent, when the lease runs out, which printer and job it covers, and who asked for it.

sections.title: The Operations
sections.content:
Six new operation identifiers are registered: 0x0016 for Create-Printer-Subscriptions, 0x0017 for Create-Job-Subscriptions, 0x0018 for Get-Subscription-Attributes, 0x0019 for Get-Subscriptions, 0x001A for Renew-Subscription and 0x001B for Cancel-Subscription. The memo also extends the existing Print-Job, Print-URI, Create-Job, Validate-Job, Get-Printer-Attributes and Restart-Job operations.

Create-Job-Subscriptions takes a notify-job-id operation attribute, which the client must supply and which must be the job-id of the job the Per-Job Subscription is to be associated with; if the client omits it the printer must reject the request with a client-error-bad-request status code. The response carries one Subscription Attributes Group per request group. A successful-ok status code means every requested Subscription Object was created, successful-ok-ignored-subscriptions means some were created and some failed, and the groups with a notify-status-code attribute are the ones that failed. A client-error-ignored-all-subscriptions status code means none were created and all failed. A client-error-not-possible error can occur because the specified job has already completed, whether or not the job is retained.

Create-Printer-Subscriptions works the same way except that it creates Per-Printer Subscription Objects associated with the printer, and its operation attributes must not contain notify-job-id. Creating Per-Printer Subscription Objects requires Operator or Administrator access rights for the printer, or authorization by the printer's administrator-configured security policy.

In a Job Creation operation the subscription template groups come after the operation attributes and, where present, after the Job Template group. The operation succeeds if and only if the job creation succeeds, and if the printer does not create some or all of the requested Subscription Objects it must return a successful-ok-ignored-subscriptions status code instead of successful-ok, but it must not reject the operation because of a failure to create Subscription Objects. If the printer does not support the notification specification at all, it treats the Subscription Attributes Group like an unknown group and ignores it, which tells the client that notification is not supported.

Validate-Job lets a client test whether Subscription Objects could be created, by supplying the same template groups. The response carries the same groups as Print-Job, except that there is no Job Object Attributes Group because no job is created, and no notify-subscription-id because no Subscription Object is created. The status codes say what would happen.

Restart-Job is neither a Job Creation operation nor a Subscription Creation operation, and the client must not supply any Job Subscription Attributes Groups. The printer reuses the existing job with the same job-id and the existing Per-Job Subscription Objects with the same subscription-ids, so it returns neither a job-id nor any Subscription Attributes groups. After the operation completes successfully the printer generates a job-created event.

Renew-Subscription asks the printer to extend the lease on a Per-Printer Subscription Object. The printer must support it, must accept the request in any of the printer's states, and must not change the printer's printer-state attribute. It must reject the request for a Per-Job Subscription Object, because that has no lease, and return client-error-not-possible. The client must supply the notify-subscription-id, and the printer returns the number of seconds it has actually granted, which may differ from the number requested.

Cancel-Subscription cancels the lease on a Per-Printer Subscription Object, and thereby deletes it, or deletes a Per-Job Subscription Object.
sections.plainLanguage: Six new operations are added: three create subscriptions, two read them back and one renews the lease. A client usually asks for a subscription in the same request that submits the print job. The printer answers with an identifier for each subscription it created, and the client uses that identifier to renew or cancel it later.

sections.title: Delivery Methods
sections.content:
A Delivery Method is the mechanism, that is the protocol, by which the printer delivers an Event Notification to a Notification Recipient. There are several potential delivery methods, standardized as well as proprietary. The specification requires that the ippget pull delivery method of RFC 3996 be supported, and conforming implementations may support additional push or pull delivery methods as well. The memo defines none of these mechanisms itself.

Each delivery method must be defined in a Delivery Method Document separate from this document, and new methods are created as needed using an extension to the registration procedures of RFC 2911, then registered with IANA.

The memo lists the sorts of delivery method that are possible: the notification recipient polls for event notifications at intervals directed by the printer, the printer delivers event notifications using HTTP as the transport, or the printer delivers an email message.

A delivery method document must contain an exact copy of the memo's paragraph, caption and table, and column 2 of the table in the delivery method document must contain answers to the questions in column 1 for that delivery method. The questions cover the URL scheme name for a push method or the keyword name for a pull method, whether the method is required, recommended or optional for an IPP printer to support, the transport and delivery protocols the printer uses and therefore the whole network stack, whether several event notifications can be combined into a Compound Event Notification, whether the method is initiated by the recipient or by the printer, whether the content is machine consumable or human consumable, which section of the memo answers the question of the representation and encoding of the notification content, the latency and reliability of the transport and delivery protocol, the security aspects of the transport and delivery protocol including how it is handled in firewalls, the content length restrictions, the additional values or pieces of information the printer delivers, and the additional subscription template and description attributes.

Each delivery method gets exactly one name, a URL scheme name for a push method or a keyword for a pull method, and the name must uniquely identify a single delivery method. Push names must follow the rules for URL scheme names and pull names the rules for keywords in RFC 2911.
sections.plainLanguage: How the message actually travels is set aside for a separate document per method. The one method every implementation must have is ippget, where the client fetches the notifications. Other methods, such as pushing over HTTP or sending email, are registered separately and each has to describe its own security and its own limits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clients submitting notification requests to an IPP printer have the same security issues as submitting a print job request, and the same mechanisms used by IPP version 1.1 can be used. Operations that require authentication can use HTTP authentication, and operations that require privacy can use HTTP over TLS. As with IPP print job objects, if there is no security on Subscription Objects, sequential assignment of subscription identifiers exposes the system to a passive traffic monitoring threat.

The access control model for Subscription Objects is the same as for Job objects. The authenticated user performing an operation must be the owner of the Subscription Object, or have Operator or Administrator access rights for the printer, or be otherwise authorized by the printer's administrator-configured security policy. Creating Per-Printer Subscription Objects requires Operator or Administrator rights, while creating Per-Job Subscription Objects also allows the job owner.

The standard security concerns, delivery to the right user, privacy of content and tamper-proof content, apply to each delivery method, and some methods are more secure than others. Each delivery method document must discuss its own security considerations.

Two specific threats are named. The first is a notification trap door: if a printer supports the optional notify-attributes attribute, where the client can ask the printer to return any specified job, printer and subscription object attributes, the printer must apply the same security policy to those requested attributes as it applies to the Get-Jobs, Get-Job-Attributes, Get-Printer-Attributes and Get-Subscription-Attributes requests.

The second is unwanted event notifications, that is spam. For any push delivery method, by far the biggest security concern is the abuse of notification, delivering unwanted event notifications to third parties. The problem is made worse by notification addresses that may be redistributed to multiple parties, and there are scenarios where third party notification is used. Any fully secure solution would require the active agreement of all recipients before delivering anything.
sections.plainLanguage: As with print jobs, a subscription can only be made or read by the right users. The memo also warns about spam, because a push method can be pointed at an address that many people receive, and a fully safe solution would need everyone to agree in advance.
